n: King Agrippa gave Paul permission to speak. Paul raised his hand in the classic gesture of an orator — likely still in chains — and began his defense.

f.g: A customary gesture of a speaker beginning an address.

n: Paul says he counts himself fortunate to defend himself before Agrippa. His courtesy is sincere, not flattering.
Agrippa was an expert in Jewish customs and debates, so Paul asks him to listen patiently. Paul knows this audience can follow his argument from scripture.
Paul begins with his life story: everyone among the Jews in Jerusalem knows how he lived from his youth.

f.w: My manner of life from my youth

n: If they were willing, they could testify that he lived as a Pharisee — the strictest party in Judaism.

f.g: The strictest party — the Pharisees were known for exacting observance.

n: Now he is on trial for his hope in the promise God made to Israel’s ancestors — the coming of the Messiah and the resurrection.

f.w: the promise made of God unto our fathers

n: All twelve tribes worship God earnestly day and night, hoping to see this promise fulfilled. The irony: Paul is accused for holding Israel’s own hope.
Paul turns to the whole audience: Why should anyone find it unbelievable that God raises the dead? For the God who created life, resurrection is not impossible.

f.w: that God should raise the dead

n: Paul admits he once felt sure it was his duty to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth. Sincerity alone doesn’t make someone right.
With the chief priests’ authority, he jailed many saints in Jerusalem and voted for their deaths.

f.w: I gave my voice against them
f.g: Literally “I cast my pebble” — cast my vote against them.
Holy ones — a common name for members of the Church.

n: He punished believers in synagogue after synagogue, tried to force them to deny their faith, and in his fury chased them to foreign cities.

f.g: Tried to force them to curse or deny Christ.

n: That’s why he was traveling to Damascus with authority from the chief priests.
At noon he saw a light from heaven brighter than the sun, shining around him and his companions.

f.w: above the brightness of the sun

n: They all fell, and Jesus spoke in Hebrew: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.” Fighting God only hurts yourself.

f.g: A proverb: an ox that kicks at the sharp goad driving it only wounds itself.

n: “Who are you, Lord?” — “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.”

f.w: I am Jesus whom thou persecutest

n: Jesus commanded Paul to stand up: I have appeared to you to make you my servant and witness of what you have seen and what I will yet show you.
The Lord promised to rescue Paul from his own people and from the Gentiles, to whom he was sending him.

f.w: unto whom now I send thee

n: Paul’s mission in one beautiful sentence: open people’s eyes, turn them from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God, so they can be forgiven and receive an inheritance among the sanctified.

f.w: sanctified by faith that is in me

n: So, King Agrippa, I did not disobey that heavenly vision. Joseph Smith later drew strength from Paul’s steadfastness in testifying of what he had seen.

f.w: I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision

n: He preached first in Damascus, then Jerusalem and Judea, then to the Gentiles: repent, turn to God, and live in a way that shows real repentance.

f.g: Live in ways that fit and prove true repentance.

n: That is why the Jews seized him in the temple and tried to kill him.
With God’s help he has survived to this day, testifying to everyone — small and great — of only what Moses and the prophets foretold. Paul is preaching fulfillment, not novelty.

f.g: Ordinary people and important people alike.

f.w: the prophets and Moses did say

n: That the Messiah would suffer, be the first to rise from the dead, and bring light to Israel and the Gentiles.

f.w: the first that should rise from the dead

n: Festus interrupted loudly: Paul, you’re out of your mind — all your learning has driven you mad! The resurrection sounded absurd to a Roman.

f.g: You are out of your mind.

n: Paul calmly replied that he wasn’t mad but was speaking true and sensible words.
The king knows about these things, Paul said; none of it happened in secret. Jesus’ ministry, death, and the rise of the Church were public events.

f.w: this thing was not done in a corner
f.g: It happened openly, not hidden away.

n: Paul pressed Agrippa directly: Do you believe the prophets? I know you do. If he did, he would have to consider their fulfillment in Jesus.
Agrippa responded, “Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian.” Many read this as a wry deflection — “In such a short time you think you can make me a Christian?”

f.w: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian
f.g: The Greek can mean “in a short time,” possibly an ironic dodge.

n: Paul’s gracious answer: whether it takes short or long, I pray to God that you and everyone here would become as I am — except for these chains.

f.g: Except for these chains — Paul spoke while bound.

n: With that, the king, the governor, Bernice, and the others rose to leave.
In private, they agreed: this man has done nothing to deserve death or prison.

f.w: nothing worthy of death or of bonds

n: Agrippa told Festus that Paul could have been freed had he not appealed to Caesar. Yet that appeal was the very path God used to bring Paul to Rome.

f.w: if he had not appealed unto Cæsar
